summary: Stress-test the two-sided talent-platform vision for missing pieces

panels.notes: The supply-side discovery surface is genuinely complete: /scout browse, filter, leaderboards, compare, watchlist with notes, CSV export, and digest emails give scouts a real discovery workflow, and reusing the pre-existing TrackedPlayer roster solves the classic empty-shelf problem — a scout landing on day one sees real, verified, provenance-clean players, not an empty directory. The trust mechanics are the strongest part: hard visual separation of self-reported vs. verified stats is exactly the right moat design, and the funding registry (PR #636) already does verified-program-only admission, evidence-based claim verification, manager grants, an audit trail, and — notably — demand counting via notify_when_fundable saves, which is real marketplace instrumentation on the supply side. Safeguarding awareness is present in the roadmap (open commentary on minor profiles deliberately deferred, mirroring the Film Room opposition-numbers-only consent posture). Admin-in-the-loop approval for both profile claims and program admission keeps verification human, which protects quality. What's missing is not the discovery half — it's everything that happens AFTER discovery.

missing.title: The loop never closes — there is no contact / introduction / trial-request rail between scouts and players
missing.why: A scout can browse, filter, shortlist, and get digests about a player — and then hit a dead end. There is no endpoint anywhere in scout.py or showcase.py that lets a scout reach a player, their agent, or their club; the only 'message' field in the whole showcase flow is the claimant's private note to the admin reviewer. So the actual valuable event (an introduction that leads to a trial or signing) happens entirely off-platform, on Instagram DM or email. Either you build a governed contact rail or you are a data-lookup tool, not a marketplace — and a scout has no reason to pay for Scout Pro when 'export the CSV and DM them myself' is free and does the same job.
missing.evidence: academy-watch-backend/src/routes/scout.py and showcase.py — endpoints cover watchlist/compare/digest/claim/reel; no contact, inquiry, introduction, or trial endpoint exists; MAX_MESSAGE_LENGTH is claimant-to-admin only

missing.title: No outcome tracking — nothing captures whether a listing ever led to a trial or signing
missing.why: There is no data model that records 'scout X viewed / contacted player Y' or 'this connection produced a trial/signing.' Without it you can never tell a player 'three academy scouts looked at you this week,' never tell a scout 'two players you shortlisted got signed,' and never market 'The Academy Watch generated N trials.' That is the proof the marketplace works — the social proof that drives both sides to return and the value metric you'd price a subscription on. Either you instrument outcomes (even a lightweight self-reported 'did this lead to contact?') or you are permanently blind to whether your core promise is real, and every retention and pricing decision is a guess.
missing.evidence: No outcome/interaction event model found across models/ (product_event.py is analytics telemetry, not marketplace-outcome capture)

missing.title: Adult-scout-to-minor-player contact is unspecified, and scout accounts are unvetted — a child-safety gap that must be closed before ANY contact rail ships
missing.why: The entire reason this marketplace exists is to put scouts in front of academy players, many of whom are minors. Today a watchlist requires only a generic authenticated user account — there is no 'verified scout' gate, no club-affiliation check, no identity verification. The moment you add any way to contact a player (see the first finding), you have created a channel for unvetted adults to initiate contact with children. That needs guardian-mediated routing (no direct scout-to-minor channel), scout identity verification BEFORE a scout can even see or reach a minor, and full audit logging — built before launch, not after. Either these controls exist before the contact rail goes live, or a single predatory signup becomes a safeguarding incident that ends the company overnight.
missing.evidence: scout.py watchlist endpoints use @require_user_auth (any authenticated user); no scout-verification model; ROADMAP open decision on safeguarding minors marked unresolved for P2

missing.title: The demand side (scouts) is unverified — the moat only protects the supply side
missing.why: The whole thesis is verification: real fixture stats plus club-vouched footage on the player side. But the scout side is completely unverified — anyone can register and browse. The roadmap's P2 mentions 'verified scouts/coaches' for endorsements but no scout-credential model exists. A player who exposes their profile to 'scouts' can't tell a real academy recruiter from a curious parent or a data scraper, which is both a safeguarding hole and a signal-quality problem — the exact noise players came here to escape. Either you verify the demand side (club affiliation, license, credential) so a 'scout' badge means something, or the demand side is indistinguishable from random traffic and the players' reason to be here evaporates.
missing.evidence: No scout/recruiter verification model; watchlist and export gated only on generic user auth in scout.py

missing.title: Crowdfunding donors are an unserved third side — there is no post-donation impact, update, or recognition loop
missing.why: The funding registry handles admission, claims, and demand-counting, and money movement is deferred — but the donor's ongoing relationship is entirely absent: no impact reporting ('your $50 bought a set of kits'), no program updates feed, no donor recognition/wall, no recurring-giving relationship, no receipt/acknowledgment flow. People give to youth sports for emotional connection and proof of impact, not a one-time transaction. Either you design the donor's ongoing side now, before wiring Stripe, or every donation is a one-shot — you capture a single payment instead of a recurring donor, and clubs get no feedback loop rewarding them for keeping a program active and updated.
missing.evidence: CONTINUITY_grassroots-funding.md F2 scope: registry/admission/claims/demand/audit shipped; no impact-reporting, program-update, or donor-recognition surface; money movement + donation UI deferred to F3/F4

missing.title: Cold-start: a scout browsing finds mostly unclaimed players with no reel and no contact path — the two sides don't yet bootstrap each other
missing.why: Player showcase profiles need admin-approved claims and funding programs need admin admission — both throttled by manual human review. The TrackedPlayer roster gives scouts something to browse (good), but that browseable player is usually UNCLAIMED: no curated reel, no owner, and (per the first finding) no way to act on them. So a scout sees a directory of players they can't reach, and players see no scouts arriving. Either you seed claimed, contactable profiles in a narrow beachhead (one region or league) so both sides feel populated at once, or each side shows up, finds the other side inert, and doesn't come back — the classic two-sided cold-start death.
missing.evidence: showcase.py claim flow is pending→admin-approved; CONTINUITY_grassroots-funding.md admission is admin-gated; ROADMAP notes everything today is admin/journalist-curated, not player-owned at scale

missing.title: Matching is pull-only — no way for clubs to post what they need or for players to learn anyone is looking
missing.why: Every path is scout-initiated browse-and-filter. There is no reverse channel: a club can't post 'we need a left-footed centre-back, U18, within 200km' and have matching players surface, and a player gets no signal when a scout's criteria match their profile. In marketplaces with thin liquidity, the scarcer side usually has to post demand to activate the other side. Without demand-posting and match-notification, discovery rests entirely on scouts doing manual filtering, and players remain passive with no evidence anyone is interested — leaving the players' half of the market inert even after they've claimed a profile.
missing.evidence: scout.py is entirely query/filter/leaderboard driven; follow.py is user-follows-player (inbound to scout), not a club-need posting or player-facing match notification

missing.title: Nothing keeps a successful connection on-platform — Scout Pro is a flat subscription, not tied to intros or outcomes
missing.why: Once you do build contact and outcomes, a scout and a player who connect have every incentive to move to WhatsApp and cut the platform out — and because Scout Pro is a flat monthly subscription rather than per-successful-intro, there's no economic reason for either to keep activity visible. No verified-intro record, deal history, or reputation that only accrues on-platform gives them a reason to stay. Either value accrues from staying (a verified track record, ongoing player monitoring, outcome-gated features) or the marketplace becomes a lead-gen tool people churn out of after one signing, capping lifetime value.
missing.evidence: /pricing assumes flat Scout Pro / Film Room tiers (scout_tier scaffold); no intro-record, deal-history, or on-platform reputation model exists

panels.notes: The vision shows real safeguarding instinct, and several defenses are already load-bearing. The hard visual separation of self-reported vs. verified fixture stats is a genuine misrepresentation shield — if a self-reported height or bio is false, you can point to the labelled boundary rather than owning the false claim. Pre-moderation of all owner-submitted showcase content (everything reverts to `pending` on edit) is a real safeguarding control and the correct default for a minor-heavy platform. The "donations to VERIFIED club programs only, never to individual minors" rule avoids the single worst legal trap (paying money to identifiable children / becoming their financial handler). US-only donation launch sensibly narrows the jurisdictional surface. The Apple-safe "money only moves on web" posture keeps the App Store review risk down. And the manual admin approval on `PlayerProfileClaim` is exactly the right place to bolt on the consent and identity checks the findings below call for — the hook exists, it's just empty. What is missing is almost entirely at the layer BELOW these good instincts: lawful basis, consent capture, and the statutory obligations that attach automatically the moment minors' data and footage are involved, whether or not you charge for it.

missing.title: No lawful basis or erasure path for the minors the whole platform profiles without consent
missing.why: The TrackedPlayer backbone, journey sync, verified multi-season stats and AI newsletters build detailed, named, ongoing profiles of thousands of identifiable children pulled from API-Football — none of whom (or whose parents) ever agreed. Under UK/EU GDPR you need a documented lawful basis to profile a child, and the UK Age-Appropriate Design Code treats this as high-risk by default. Either you have a written lawful-basis assessment and a working 'delete this child' process, or the first parent who emails the ICO/a takedown demand can force you to erase that player — and you currently have no mechanism to honour it or defend the processing.
missing.evidence: TrackedPlayer + journey.birth_date + academy_window.age_from_birth_date show per-child profiling; grep found no consent/lawful-basis/erasure/DSAR handling anywhere in src; CLAUDE.md states 'Many tracked players are MINORS'.

missing.title: Film Room footage captures opposition minors who never consented — image rights + child-data exposure
missing.why: A match video films BOTH teams. The clips you cut, verify and attach to showcase profiles will contain other clubs' 14-16-year-olds whose parents never agreed to appear in a commercial product. That is a personal-image/publicity-rights problem AND child-data processing on kids you have no relationship with. Either you get a consent/opt-out mechanism and blur/withhold non-consenting minors, or one complaint from an opposing parent forces takedown of clips, poisons the club relationships you depend on, and undermines the very clip library you plan to sell at ~$25/match.
missing.evidence: Task brief: 'match footage containing minors (both teams — opposition players did not consent)'; Film Room CV pipeline (jersey OCR + per-player clips) confirmed as designed feature; no consent model in schema.

missing.title: Minor self-registration has no age gate, verifiable parental consent, or identity verification
missing.why: PlayerProfileClaim.relationship_type includes 'player', so a child can claim and self-report on their own profile, and admin approval captures no consent and no proof the claimant is who they say. Two hard problems collide: (1) the FTC's amended COPPA Rule is in FULL force as of April 2026 — once a US under-13 self-registers you are an operator with actual knowledge and owe verifiable parental consent you don't collect; and (2) with no identity check, an adult stranger can claim a real named minor's page ('agent'/'guardian') — a safeguarding nightmare. Either the claim flow gates on age and captures verifiable parental consent + relationship proof, or you are simultaneously exposed to FTC penalties and to a predator obtaining a curated page tied to a specific child.
missing.evidence: showcase.py PlayerProfileClaim: relationship_type player|agent|guardian|club_official, status pending→approved, no DOB/consent/identity fields; COPPA amended rule full effect 22 Apr 2026 (FTC, Federal Register 2025-05904).

missing.title: Donation flow triggers 40-state charitable-solicitation + platform registration and a deceptive-'donation' risk
missing.why: Soliciting US donations means registering as a charitable solicitor in ~40 states, AND California's charitable-fundraising-platform law (AB 488, live since 2023) requires the PLATFORM itself to register with the CA AG, obtain each recipient charity's written consent, and disclose fees before it may facilitate a single donation. Separately: if a 'verified club program' is actually a for-profit academy, calling the payment a 'donation' and implying tax-deductibility is a deceptive practice, and skimming a platform 'operating percentage' off charitable gifts must be disclosed. Either you build charity-status verification (real 501(c)(3) check), state/AB-488 registration, and clear fee/deductibility disclosure into the funding registry, or a state AG can shut the donation product down and treat the fee-skim as consumer fraud.
missing.evidence: Task brief: donations to verified programs, platform takes a percentage, Stripe Connect US-only; funding registry shipped PR #636; CA AB 488 charitable fundraising platform rules; multi-state charitable solicitation registration regime.

missing.title: No illegal-content (CSAM) detection or mandatory-reporting mechanism on user/club uploads about minors
missing.why: You will host user-uploaded video and images centred on children (club match uploads, claim submissions). US law makes reporting to NCMEC mandatory the moment a provider obtains actual knowledge of child sexual abuse material, and the UK Online Safety Act imposes active child-safety and illegal-content duties on user-to-user services. With a 'verified club uploads video' pipeline and a public claim system, you have an upload surface and zero detection/reporting layer. Either you add illegal-content scanning/hash-matching, a notice-and-takedown route, and a NCMEC/reporting process, or a single malicious upload leaves you criminally and regulatorily exposed with no defensible process.
missing.evidence: Film Room club video upload + PlayerProfileClaim submissions = UGC surface about minors; US 18 U.S.C. 2258A NCMEC reporting duty; UK Online Safety Act 2023 child-safety duties; no moderation/reporting layer found in models.

missing.title: Reselling API-Football data inside a PAID product likely breaches its redistribution license
missing.why: API-Football is your SOLE stats source, and its terms restrict redistributing/reselling the underlying data. The planned Scout Pro paid tiers surface exactly that data to paying customers, which is the classic 'you may consume but not resell our feed' line. Either you confirm in writing that your plan (paid access to their stats, cached and stored in Supabase) is licensed at the right tier, or the provider can terminate you for breach — and because they are your only data source, that single termination takes down loan tracking, stats, newsletters and Scout Desk at once.
missing.evidence: CLAUDE.md: 'API-Football (all football data)'; api_cache stores/redistributes their data; paid Scout tier scaffold (scout_tier entitlement, /pricing) per task brief.

missing.title: Facilitating scout-to-minor contact can breach football-governance approach/tapping rules
missing.why: The Scout Desk connects scouts (who often act for clubs) with young players tied to OTHER academies. FIFA's protection-of-minors regime (RSTP Art. 19) and national association 'approach/tapping-up' rules restrict contacting another club's registered minor — and the platform becomes the tool of any improper approach. The FIFA Football Agent Regulations are currently SUSPENDED under an EU injunction, so the acute agent-licensing risk is lower today, but national intermediary rules and the minor-approach rules are live. Either you keep the product to passive discovery/watchlists (no facilitated introductions to another club's registered minor) with clear terms, or clubs whose players get approached through your tool complain to their FA and refuse to work with you.
missing.evidence: Scout Desk comparisons/leaderboards + follow/contact intent; FIFA FFAR suspended pending CJEU (Dortmund/Düsseldorf injunction upheld 2024, still suspended July 2026); FIFA RSTP Art.19 minor-protection rules remain in force.

panels.notes: Several instincts here are right and worth protecting. (1) The "free discovery feeds paid workflow" funnel logic on the /pricing page is sound SaaS structure — a free Scout Standard tier that seeds the graph and upsells Pro is the correct shape, not cannibalization, PROVIDED the paid tier lands on a segment that actually has budget (see findings). (2) The Apple-safe posture — all money movement on web, iOS shows informational badges only — correctly dodges Apple's 30% IAP tax on subscriptions and donations; do not let anyone "simplify" this by adding in-app purchase later. (3) Pay-per-match for Film Room (usage-based, not flat) is the right meter for a variable-cost CV+human-review pipeline — it avoids the trap of an all-you-can-eat plan that loses money on heavy users. (4) The "never to individual minors, verified club programs only" donation rule is the correct trust/legal spine and is genuinely differentiating. The gaps below are about which rail to turn on first, who is actually holding the credit card, and two reputational/contractual landmines in the money flows.

missing.title: The revenue model charges the wrong side: the segment with proven willingness-to-pay (exposure-seekers) is kept free, the side you meter (scouts) has the least budget
missing.why: Real market pricing shows where money is: parents/families pay recruiting platforms $2,500–5,000/yr (NCSA) and clubs pay $1,500–3,000/team (SportsRecruits) specifically for EXPOSURE — getting a young player seen. Meanwhile pro-club scouts, the segment Scout Pro targets, already have Wyscout/Hudl budgets ($325–400/yr individual, custom for orgs) and amateur scouts have near-zero willingness-to-pay. So the platform gives the showcase side (players/clubs listing themselves — the exposure-seekers with proven WTP) away free forever, and tries to monetize scouts, who either won't pay or are already spending their budget elsewhere. Either you find a paid exposure product for the player/club side (featured placement, verified-profile boost, digest inclusion) that does not violate pay-to-play, or Scout Pro subscription revenue stays near zero and you have monetized the one side of a two-sided market that has no money.
missing.evidence: NCSA $2,500–5,000/yr and SportsRecruits $1,500–3,000/team (recruiting-exposure WTP); Wyscout/Hudl $325–400/yr individual (scout-side budget already committed); repo /pricing page keeps Scout Standard + showcase free, meters Scout Pro + Film Room

missing.title: Mandatory platform fee skimmed off youth-club donations is a reputational landmine with a zero-fee benchmark staring at it
missing.why: The plan takes 'a small operating percentage' off crowdfunding that flows to youth football programs. GoFundMe charges 0% platform fee on exactly this category (only pass-through card processing ~2.9%+$0.30); Zeffy markets 0% for youth/school teams. The moment a journalist or parent writes 'tech startup skims a cut off donations meant for kids' academy football,' the verification/trust moat — the entire thesis — is damaged, and no disclaimer undoes the headline. Either restructure the fee as an OPTIONAL donor tip (GoFundMe/Givebutter model: donor chooses to cover platform costs on top, club receives 100%), or you have built a revenue rail whose optics can poison the brand that the rest of the product depends on.
missing.evidence: GoFundMe 0% platform fee on sports fundraisers; Zeffy 0% for schools/teams; Givebutter/RallyUp optional-tip model eliminates platform fee; donations target verified minor-serving club programs

missing.title: Wire Film Room first — but only after identity-merge quality clears a bar, and re-price it: ~$25/match likely sells a broken deliverable below cost
missing.why: Of the three unwired rails, Film Room has the clearest buyer (verified clubs, already onboarded) and a tangible deliverable, so it should be first to bill. But two things break it: (a) the documented core R&D risk is that only ~14% of players get correctly named — charging $25 for a per-player report that misattributes clips destroys trust on the exact evidence the moat is built on; bill only once accuracy is defensible, or offer it concierge-free until then. (b) $25/match must cover CV compute PLUS human tag review labor PLUS Stripe fees — Veo's whole-club economics run $800–1,300/yr for automated recording with NO human review step, so $25 for a labor-touched per-match report is probably underwater. Either raise the per-match price (or bundle it, see below) and gate billing behind an accuracy threshold, or you scale a rail that loses money per unit and erodes trust per report.
missing.evidence: Veo Essential $804/yr, Pro $1,308/yr (automated, no human review); repo notes ~14% players correctly named + human tag-review step in pipeline; designed price ~$25/match

missing.title: Missing rail: a recurring club SaaS bundle — the verified-club assets are being sold as one-off transactions instead of a subscription
missing.why: Verified clubs get three things — the funding registry (PR #636), Film Room, and roster/showcase tools — but each is transactional or free. Veo proves clubs pay $800–1,300/yr RECURRING for a single capability (recording). Bundling funding-registry access + a monthly Film Room match allotment + roster management into one annual club plan converts unpredictable pay-per-match into predictable MRR, raises switching cost, and lets you price on total value (fundraising + analytics + visibility) rather than per-match compute. Either package a club tier, or you leave the most durable, highest-retention revenue in the portfolio unbuilt while chasing per-transaction dollars.
missing.evidence: Veo $804–1,308/yr recurring per club; SportsRecruits $1,500–3,000/team; repo has funding registry (PR #636) + Film Room + showcase all sold separately/free

missing.title: Scout Pro is 'free during beta, price at launch' with no committed number and no billing wired — a free-tier trap that trains users to expect $0
missing.why: The /pricing page shows Scout Pro as 'Free during beta / pricing announced at launch' with the full Pro feature set already unlocked for free. Every month this ships, the beta cohort anchors on $0 for the exact workflow you intend to charge for; when a paywall finally drops, conversion craters and you get a churn event instead of revenue. TransferRoom and Wyscout never let their core audience use the paid product free indefinitely. Either commit a launch price and a grandfather/trial-conversion path NOW (e.g. 'Pro is $X/yr from [date]; beta users get 50% for year one'), or you are manufacturing a future cliff where your most engaged users leave the moment they are asked to pay.
missing.evidence: repo PricingPage.jsx: Scout Pro priceLine 'Free during beta', priceNote 'pricing announced at launch', full Pro feature list already active

missing.title: Missing rail: agent-side monetization is where transfer money actually sits — and it's the pay-to-play landmine the constraint half-anticipates
missing.why: Agents are the one segment in youth football with both cash and direct financial motive (they profit from transfers), and TransferRoom monetizes exactly them via mandatory annual fees + paid PlayerMarket add-ons. The platform has verified stats + showcase profiles agents would pay to access or to boost their players into — but charging an agent to elevate a MINOR's visibility is the definition of pay-to-play the owner has explicitly ruled out. This needs a deliberate line, not silence: e.g. agents pay for SCOUT-side discovery/search tools (finding talent) but can never buy placement/ranking for a player. Either design an agent product that stays the right side of that line, or you either leave the niche's richest payer entirely unmonetized, or drift into pay-to-play by accident.
missing.evidence: TransferRoom monetizes agents via annual fee + PlayerMarket paid add-on; platform's explicit 'must not become pay-to-play' constraint; many tracked players are minors

missing.title: A data-licensing rail exists in the dataset but is contractually fenced by API-Football's terms — an unexamined opportunity AND risk
missing.why: The platform has assembled something sellable: verified multi-season stats + journey/pathway classification across 16 leagues, structured and de-duplicated — media, agencies, and other clubs pay for exactly this kind of clean dataset. But API-Football is the sole upstream and its terms almost certainly prohibit redistribution or resale of derived data, so licensing it out could breach the supplier contract and cut off the data spine the whole product runs on. Either read the API-Football license and confirm what derived/aggregated data you may resell (it may permit your own-analysis outputs while forbidding raw redistribution), or you are sitting on a revenue rail you legally can't turn on — and possibly already skating close to a term violation with the public stat pages.
missing.evidence: API-Football is sole external provider (per CLAUDE.md, crawl scope env-gated); redistribution/resale clauses standard in sports-data licenses; platform holds derived multi-season + journey-classified data across 16 leagues

panels.notes: The genuinely unoccupied ground is real and the vision is pointed at it: no incumbent combines club-verified scouting data + a funding rail + safe handling of under-18s. TransferRoom is 18-and-over only and pro-club-facing; Wyscout/Hudl is expensive and built for pro recruiters, not funding or minors; Tonsser is self-reported and unverified; Snap! Raise and Vertical Raise do youth fundraising with zero football/scouting context and no club-verification. The "donations only to a verified club program, never to a minor" design is a differentiator none of the money platforms have, and the loan-journey / academy-pathway tracking backbone is a genuinely distinctive angle nobody else frames this way. The Apple-safe "all money on web, badges-only in the app" posture is also correctly ahead of where Tonsser and TransferRoom sit. So the integration thesis is defensible in principle — the risk is entirely in execution depth per pillar, because each individual pillar already has a deeper, funded incumbent (below).

missing.title: Hudl/Wyscout already owns the exact 'verified footage → scouting database' moat this vision claims
missing.why: The pitch is that the moat is verification: real fixture stats plus club-vouched footage beating Instagram reels. But Hudl now owns Wyscout (the world's largest soccer scouting database, used by Premier League/La Liga/Serie A scouts) AND the Focus camera, and starting the 2026-27 season Focus match video flows automatically into Wyscout with every youth player individually auto-tagged, xG, heatmaps, and a permanent searchable record — that IS club-verified footage feeding a scouting DB, at professional scale, already live for US youth (ECNL). Either The Academy Watch names a verification layer Wyscout structurally cannot copy (funding, sub-18 safety, loan pathway), or a scout who can pull auto-tagged verified youth footage from Wyscout has no reason to open The Academy Watch and the headline moat is already occupied.
missing.evidence: Hudl.com Focus→Wyscout League Exchange auto-flow (2026-27); ECNL first US youth league in Wyscout with per-athlete auto-tagging; Wyscout advanced metrics (xG, duels, heatmaps)

missing.title: Sole reliance on API-Football leaves the 'real fixture stats' moat empty for the actual academy/youth segment it targets
missing.why: API-Football covers professional league fixtures. It does not cover most academy, reserve, or grassroots youth matches — which is exactly the young-talent population the platform is built around. Incumbents solved this by deriving stats from the footage itself: Wyscout ingests the largest youth-competition catalog in the world, and Veo/Trace generate per-player stats straight off the grassroots match they filmed. So for a 15-year-old academy prospect, The Academy Watch has no verified fixture stats to show unless that player has already appeared in a covered senior pro league. Either the platform adds a footage-derived or partner-fed stat source for sub-pro football, or its verification promise collapses precisely where its users live and it can only verify players who are already visible elsewhere.
missing.evidence: API-Football pro-league scope (16 leagues configured); Wyscout 'largest number of youth competitions in the world'; Trace/Veo footage-derived per-player stats

missing.title: No capture/hardware layer — the Film Room is downstream of cameras (Veo, Trace, Pixellot) that already own the flywheel
missing.why: Film Room needs clubs to upload match video into a concierge CV pipeline at ~$25/match. But 40,000+ clubs already film with Veo, and Veo/Trace/Pixellot auto-generate player highlights and are one click from Wyscout — the club gets clips and data as a byproduct of the camera it already bought. A verified club deciding where its footage and player data live will keep it where the camera, the highlights, and the scout network already are. Either The Academy Watch integrates with (ingests from) those camera ecosystems instead of asking clubs to re-upload into a separate paid pipeline, or the analytics pillar competes for a second upload clubs have no reason to do, and the documented player-identity-merge R&D risk buys a capability the camera vendors already ship.
missing.evidence: Veo 40,000+ clubs; Trace auto individual-player highlights for recruitment; Focus→Wyscout auto-flow removes the upload step entirely

missing.title: Tonsser is a free, 2M-user incumbent on the player self-listing side, and its 'scouts pay' model is the same revenue the pricing page assumes
missing.why: The player showcase (claimed profile, highlight reels, bio, self-reported attributes, trials/discovery) is Tonsser's exact product — 'LinkedIn for youth football,' 2M+ players, VC-funded, with resume, stats, video, trial applications, a following feed, and its revenue already coming from scouts and clubs paying for access plus parent subscriptions. A young player deciding where to build a profile picks the network with 2M peers and existing scout attention. The Academy Watch's differentiator has to be verification depth — but per the two findings above that depth is thin without youth fixture stats. Either the platform can show a scout something verifiable that a self-reported Tonsser profile cannot, or it is a smaller, later Tonsser competing for the same scout dollars against an established two-sided network.
missing.evidence: Tonsser 2M+ users, trials/resume/discovery feature parity; revenue = scouts pay for access + club partnerships + parent subscriptions

missing.title: The crowdfunding pillar has verified supply (clubs) but no described demand engine — Snap! Raise wins by mobilizing each kid's family network
missing.why: Snap! Raise dominates US youth-sports fundraising because its mechanic is roster-driven: every athlete emails and texts their own family/friends network in a time-boxed 28-day campaign, and the program keeps ~80%. Money appears because the participants pull it from networks they already have. The Academy Watch's model is donations to verified club programs — but nothing in the vision describes who the donors are or what mobilizes them (no roster-outreach engine, no supporter/alumni acquisition loop, no campaign mechanic). Verifying clubs solves trust on the supply side; it does not create demand. Either the platform builds a donor-mobilization mechanic (supporter networks, campaign cadence, roster-driven outreach adapted to a minor-safe frame), or verified clubs list programs that raise nothing while Snap! Raise keeps the actual dollars.
missing.evidence: Snap! Raise participant email/text outreach + 28-day campaign model, ~80% retained; Vertical Raise same roster-outreach mechanic

missing.title: Any upmarket move into loan/transfer intelligence collides head-on with TransferRoom's monetized network
missing.why: The shipped loan-tracking backbone (journey sync, pathway classification, loan destinations) is an observational, journalistic version of the products TransferRoom already sells to 800+ clubs and 500+ agencies: Loan Destination Finder, Predicted Requirements, Expected Transfer Value, agent PlayerMarket. If The Academy Watch ever tries to charge clubs or agents for loan/pathway intelligence, TransferRoom is the incumbent with the transaction network and the paid data products. The genuine whitespace is the sub-18 academy layer TransferRoom deliberately excludes (players must be 18+). Either the platform stays disciplined about owning the under-18 pre-professional layer as its defensible lane, or it drifts upmarket into a fight it cannot win against an entrenched club-to-club network.
missing.evidence: TransferRoom 800+ clubs / 500+ agencies, Loan Destination Finder, Predicted Requirements, ETV, PlayerMarket; players-side 18+ only

missing.title: No stated wedge — the integration is the bet, but no single pillar is currently strong enough to win a beachhead
missing.why: The vision is four pillars (scout database, self-listing, funding, film-room analytics) and the strategic value is the combination — which is correct, because the combination is the whitespace no incumbent occupies. But each pillar individually loses to a deeper, funded incumbent (Wyscout, Tonsser, Snap! Raise, TransferRoom/Veo). A four-front simultaneous build against four different specialists, as a solo founder, with no articulated 'which pillar earns the first paying cohort and pulls the others in' sequencing, risks being second-best at everything and first at nothing. Either the roadmap names one beachhead — most plausibly the sub-18 verified-club funding rail, since that pillar's incumbents (Snap! Raise) have zero football-verification and TransferRoom/Wyscout have zero funding — and sequences the rest off its traction, or effort spreads across four fronts and none reaches the depth needed to displace its incumbent.
missing.evidence: Four-pillar scope vs. four distinct entrenched incumbents; solo-founder constraint; funding+verification+minor-safety is the one combination no competitor holds

panels.notes: The repo is far more built-out than the owner's summary implies, and the parts that touch money and minors are unusually disciplined. What's genuinely covered well: (1) The grassroots-funding design (ledgers/CONTINUITY_grassroots-funding.md) is exceptionally rigorous on money movement — verified-programs-only recipients, hard prohibition on any individual/minor/coach/parent recipient, donor-paid vs program-transfer-confirmed as separate states, dual replay-safe webhooks, de-verification/quarantine flow, default-deny RLS on every financial table, and an explicit "must model unit economics before live keys" gate. (2) Film Room's minors posture is thoughtfully handled — own-team-only reports, opposition stays anonymous, DPIA-before-processing, consent attestation, retention/deletion of recognizable footage at 90d, and metrics-honesty rules that refuse to fabricate distance/speed until homography lands (ledgers/CONTINUITY_video-analysis.md). (3) The self-reported-vs-verified separation is enforced structurally, not just visually (docs/showcase.md; models/showcase.py). (4) Engineering invariants (guarded DDL, same-migration RLS, one-head migration chain, no bulk work on the tiny prod container) are real and audited. (5) CAN-SPAM unsubscribe tokens already exist on subscriptions (models/league.py:318). The gaps below are mostly about the connective tissue and legal obligations AROUND this strong core, not the core itself.

missing.title: No self-serve account deletion or data-subject-request (access/export/erasure) tooling
missing.why: Every real user account (scouts, claimed players, agents, guardians) can create data — watchlists, follow lists, claims, self-reported bios, digest email subscriptions, analytics events — but there is no way for them to delete their account or get/erase their data. The only DELETE-account route (routes/user.py:39) is unauthenticated, targets the boilerplate User model (not the real UserAccount), and isn't even registered in main.py. Under UK GDPR / EU GDPR / California CCPA, a user (or a minor's guardian) who emails 'delete my data' has a legal right to erasure, and you have no button and no rail to honor it — every request becomes a manual database surgery, and ignoring one is a regulatory complaint. Either build a DSR/deletion path now, or you are one angry user away from a data-protection filing.
missing.why_short: No way for users or guardians to delete an account or exercise GDPR/CCPA rights; the only delete route is unauth'd and hits the wrong model.
missing.evidence: routes/user.py:39-44 (unauth DELETE on boilerplate User); main.py:100-121 (user_bp not registered); no grep hits for erasure/data_export/gdpr in src/; UserAccount holds watchlists/claims/follows/shadows (models/user.py, models/showcase.py, models/follow.py)

missing.title: Worldwide shadow tracking mints profiles and stores stats of players (many minors) with no consent, opt-out, or takedown
missing.why: Following any player who isn't already tracked mints a PlayerShadow and pulls their profile + season stats from API-Football into player_shadow_stats — worldwide, on a scout's action alone (docs/follow-graph.md §3). Many of these are minors. There is no consent step, no way for that player/guardian to see they've been indexed, no opt-out, and no per-player takedown path. The Film Room track carefully solved exactly this problem (own-team-only, consent attestation, DPIA) — but shadow tracking quietly does the opposite: it builds a global dossier on named minors as a side effect of a scout clicking 'follow'. Either add an opt-out/takedown and minimize what's stored on unclaimed minors, or a single 'why do you have a stats page on my 15-year-old' complaint becomes a safeguarding and privacy incident with your name on it.
missing.why_short: Following any untracked player builds a stored stats profile on them (often minors) worldwide with no consent, opt-out, or takedown — the opposite of Film Room's careful posture.
missing.evidence: docs/follow-graph.md §3 (shadow mint on follow, player_shadow_stats); services/player_shadow_service.py; contrast ledgers/CONTINUITY_video-analysis.md (consent/DPIA for own-team-only). No takedown/opt-out route found for shadow players.

missing.title: No connection/contact rail between scouts and the players/clubs who list themselves
missing.why: The whole two-sided thesis is 'scouts discover talent; players and clubs list themselves.' But there is no messaging, contact-request, or introduction feature anywhere in the backend — a scout who finds a player has no on-platform way to reach them, and a club has no way to respond. That means the actual valuable transaction (scout wants this kid) happens off-platform via DMs, so you capture none of it, get no data on what discovery led to, and — critically — have zero control over adults contacting minors, which is the single most-scrutinized interaction in youth football. Either design a safeguarded contact/intro flow (guardian-gated for minors) or accept that you're building a discovery engine whose payoff moment always leaks to Instagram.
missing.why_short: Discovery + verification exist, but there's no way for a scout to contact a player/club (or vice versa) on-platform — the marketplace's payoff moment leaks off-platform and dodges minor-safeguarding controls.
missing.evidence: No contact/inquiry/message endpoints in src/routes/ (grep empty); showcase claim flow (docs/showcase.md) ends at a public profile with no contact affordance; ROADMAP_talent-showcase-vision.md P2 defers even commentary.

missing.title: No notification delivery infrastructure beyond manually-triggered email digests
missing.why: Almost every 'notify' the product promises has no delivery mechanism. The weekly digest only sends when an admin manually hits an endpoint (no scheduler exists until the unbuilt Phase 3). Transactional moments — claim approved/rejected, a moderated profile edit going live, a followed player who just played, a saved program becoming fundable — have nowhere to go: follows.notify_when_fundable is a stored flag that nothing reads to send anything (ledgers/CONTINUITY_grassroots-funding.md). And despite a native iOS app in development, there's no push/APNS/device-token code at all. So users act (claim a profile, save a program, follow a prospect) and then hear nothing, which quietly kills the engagement loop the whole platform runs on. Either stand up a notification service + scheduler, or the follow/claim/save features are write-only.
missing.why_short: Digests only send on manual admin trigger (no scheduler), transactional events have no delivery, notify_when_fundable is stored-but-never-fired, and there's no iOS push despite the app.
missing.evidence: docs/follow-graph.md §2 (admin-triggered send-digests only); CONTINUITY_talent-platform-next.md §3 (scheduler is unbuilt Phase 3); CONTINUITY_grassroots-funding.md (notify_when_fundable = stored intent); no apns/device_token/push grep hits in src/

missing.title: No verified-stat rail for the grassroots / non-API-Football clubs the funding registry is built to serve
missing.why: API-Football is the sole stats provider and covers 16 pro leagues. The funding registry (PR #636) explicitly admits grassroots programs 'absent from API-Football' and non-US clubs. Those exact clubs — the ones you're asking to fundraise — get a profile page with zero verified player data, because the only non-API path is Film Room, which is concierge-only, billing-unwired, and gated on the documented identity-merge R&D risk. The 'manual player' mechanism that exists is journalist-only and still can't fetch stats (can_fetch_stats=False). So the verification moat that justifies donations ('real stats, not Instagram reels') structurally does not reach the grassroots clubs the crowdfunding feature targets. Either build a manual/attested match-data entry rail with clear provenance labeling, or the funding registry sells trust it can't deliver for its own audience.
missing.why_short: Grassroots/non-API-Football clubs (exactly who the funding registry admits) have no verified-stat path — the only options are pro-league API coverage or concierge-only, unbilled, R&D-blocked Film Room.
missing.evidence: CLAUDE.md (API-Football sole provider, 16 leagues); CONTINUITY_grassroots-funding.md (programs 'absent from API-Football', three-tier provenance ladder assumes a self-reported tier with no data-entry surface); routes/journalist.py:3364 (manual player is journalist-only); api.py:9517 (negative IDs = no stats)

missing.title: Moderation is single-admin, pre-publication only, with no user-facing abuse/impersonation reporting
missing.why: Every trust-critical decision funnels through one admin API key: claim approvals, profile-edit pre-moderation, reel-link review, club-program claims/evidence, Film Room roster linking, community takes. There are no multi-moderator roles, no triage or SLA, and — the sharp gap — no way for a user to report bad content after it's live (grep for report_abuse/flag_content is empty). As players and clubs self-list at scale, one person becomes the bottleneck, and volume pressure on a solo approver is exactly how a minor's mis-claimed or impersonated profile slips through. Worse, if someone claims a kid's profile who shouldn't, or misuses a live profile, there's no button for anyone to flag it — it sits until the admin happens to notice. Either add reviewer roles + a user report/takedown queue, or moderation quality collapses the moment self-listing works.
missing.why_short: All moderation is one admin key, pre-publication only; no reviewer roles, no SLA, and no user-facing way to report/flag live content (e.g. an impersonated minor's profile).
missing.evidence: routes/showcase.py (8 require_api_key admin surfaces); docs/showcase.md (admin manually approves claims); CONTINUITY_grassroots-funding.md (admin-only claim/evidence review); no report_abuse/flag_content/takedown grep hits in src/routes/

missing.title: The owner is under-counting shipped product — several live capabilities are absent from the vision
missing.why: The articulation omits things already in production that materially change positioning and what Scout Pro can charge for: (1) worldwide shadow tracking — scouts can follow and get pages for ANY player on earth, not just the tracked academy universe; (2) deterministic player_pulse milestone detection + cached AI-generated player cards in digests (PR #569), a real differentiator over a static list; (3) a cookieless, privacy-conscious product-analytics pipeline (PR #568) that can inform pricing decisions; (4) Dream XI / formation building; (5) GOL scouting-bot helpers (find_similar_players, find_hidden_talent, suggest_loan_destinations). Knowing you already ship these matters because you may be pricing Scout Pro against a feature set you're mentally undercounting, and because a couple of them (shadow tracking, AI cards) are the most demo-able things you have. Not urgent — but worth pulling into the pitch and the pricing page before wiring billing.
missing.why_short: Live-but-unmentioned: worldwide shadow tracking, player_pulse + cached AI player cards, cookieless analytics, Dream XI, GOL scouting helpers — all shipped and relevant to Scout Pro packaging.
missing.evidence: docs/follow-graph.md §3 (shadow tracking); CONTINUITY_talent-platform-next.md §3 (pulse+cards PR #569, analytics PR #568); routes/formation.py + routes/gol.py registered in main.py:114-116; MEMORY project_gol_scouting_helpers

panels.notes: The follow graph is genuinely strong and often the hard part: FollowList supports heterogeneous follows (player / academy_club / geo / saved-query), and following an out-of-universe player mints a lightweight PlayerShadow so worldwide players get a working page with no crawl — that's real marketplace depth. The digest delta engine is also good content-wise: it computes per-player goal/assist/minutes deltas against a per-user snapshot baseline, emits "+2 goals" chips and pulse cards, and handles dynamic (geo/query) sets via FollowPlayerSnapshot. Newsletter web pages carry a full, correct OpenGraph/Twitter-card meta block (og:image with width/height, article:author), and the PublicFormationBuilder already has a working "copy share link" — so the team understands shareable assets in principle. The claim → admin-approval → verified-vs-self-reported visual separation is the right trust spine. The problem is not content quality or the data model; it's that almost none of it is wired into a returning loop.

missing.title: Nothing brings a claimed player back — no 'who viewed / scouts watching you' signal
missing.why: A player claims their showcase profile once, then has zero reason to ever return: there is no profile-view counter, no 'a scout added you to a watchlist', no interest notification anywhere in the codebase (no view-tracking columns, no notification model). In a two-sided marketplace the listed side goes dark the moment they've filled in their reel — and a graveyard of stale profiles is exactly what makes scouts leave too. Either players get a recurring reason to open the app (someone is watching you), or side B decays to a one-time data-entry chore and the marketplace has supply that never comes back.
missing.evidence: No profile_view/view_count/viewed_by anywhere in models; no notification model exists (only admin_notify_service). scout_watchlist and follows tables record scout intent but nothing surfaces it to the followed player.

missing.title: Scout digest never fires on its own — no scheduler and no real-time alert when a followed player performs
missing.why: The only way a digest goes out today is an admin hitting the /scout endpoint by hand (send_scout_digests is admin-triggered; the model comment says 'cadence stored for a future scheduler; Phase 1 sends stay admin-triggered'; code refers to a Phase-3 scheduler that does not exist). So a scout who followed a player gets nothing automatically — not a weekly email, and certainly not a same-day 'your player scored / made his debut' alert. The single strongest weekly-return hook in this domain (a kid you're tracking just scored) is computed by the delta engine but never delivered. Either the send loop gets automated, or the whole follow/watchlist feature produces no recurring touch and scouts forget the product exists between manual sends.
missing.evidence: scout.py:1248 send_scout_digests is behind an admin route; follow.py FollowList.cadence comment 'Phase 1 sends stay admin-triggered'; scout.py:1908 'until the Phase-3 scheduler exists'. No apscheduler/cron wiring found.

missing.title: No shareable verified player card — the one native viral loop is absent
missing.why: The obvious organic-acquisition engine here is a player posting their verified card (real fixture stats + club-vouched footage) to Instagram/TikTok — exactly the 'vs self-reported Instagram reel' wedge the trust thesis is built on. But there is no shareable card asset and no per-player OpenGraph image: player and showcase pages have no og:image at all (only the newsletter template does), so even a pasted link renders as a blank card. Every player who shares their profile is free, pre-qualified traffic that also flatters the platform's verification story. Either a branded, downloadable/linkable verified card exists, or the product's single best free growth channel — proud teenagers showing off legitimate stats — is left entirely on the table.
missing.evidence: Per-player og:image absent in routes/players.py and routes/showcase.py; OG meta exists only in templates/newsletter_web.html and the static index.html sitewide default; no share-card/OG generation code found.

missing.title: Player showcase and player pages are invisible to Google — no sitemap, no prerender
missing.why: The AI newsletters and thousands of player pages are the natural top-of-funnel: someone searches a young player's name and should land on your verified page. But the site is a pure client-rendered SPA with no sitemap and no server-side prerender (no sitemap/SSR/render_to_string anywhere), so search engines see an empty shell and none of it ranks. That turns a genuine content moat — verified multi-season stats on players nobody else covers in depth — into pages no one can discover. Either player/showcase/newsletter pages get crawlable HTML (prerender + a sitemap), or you pay for every visitor forever while your best organic asset stays dark.
missing.evidence: No sitemap or SSR/prerender found in backend; player pages served from the React SPA; newsletter_web is a Flask template (crawlable) but individual player/showcase routes are SPA-only.

missing.title: The newsletter/journalist layer is disconnected from the two-sided marketplace
missing.why: You already publish AI newsletters with journalist commentary — the highest-traffic, most-shareable surface — but nothing in that reader flow pushes toward the marketplace actions that make money: no 'follow this player', 'claim this profile', or 'this player is on Manchester City's academy — see his verified page' bridge from newsletter to follow/claim. A reader finishes an article and leaves instead of becoming a follower (scout supply) or triggering a claim (player supply). Either newsletters convert their audience into marketplace participants with in-content CTAs and player-page deep links, or your biggest distribution channel and your revenue engine stay in separate universes.
missing.evidence: Newsletter routes/templates exist with proper OG meta but no follow/claim CTA wiring; follow and showcase blueprints are separate surfaces with no cross-linking found.

missing.title: No success-story / outcome loop to compound trust and re-engagement
missing.why: The most persuasive growth fuel in a scouting product is proof it works: 'this academy player was tracked here, then signed / trialed / called up.' There's no mechanism to capture or publish outcomes — no 'signed' milestone surfaced from the journey sync into a shareable story, no notification back to the scout who spotted them first. That story is what convinces the next player to claim, the next scout to pay, and the next club to register — and it's also a natural share moment. Either outcomes get captured and published as recurring proof, or every new user has to take the platform's value on faith with no evidence flywheel.
missing.evidence: journey sync classifies pathway status (signed/loan/sold transitions exist in transfer_resolver/journey_sync) but no code surfaces these as success-story content or milestone notifications; no success/outcome publication surface found.

missing.title: Registered clubs have no self-serve reason to return between concierge deliveries
missing.why: Clubs register in the funding registry (PR #636) and Film Room analytics is concierge-only, so a club's only touch with the product is when you manually hand them a report or a donation lands. There's no club-facing dashboard for 'new analytics ready', donation totals/donor activity, or profile-view stats on their program page — so the account goes cold between rare human-delivered events. As crowdfunding and pay-per-match come online, the club needs a live reason to log in (money moving in, new footage processed). Either clubs get a recurring self-serve dashboard, or the club side of the marketplace only re-engages when you personally poke it, which does not scale.
missing.evidence: Film Room documented as concierge-only; funding registry shipped as PR #636; no club dashboard for donations/analytics-ready/view-stats found among routes.

critic.notes: The six prior analysts covered the two-sided-market mechanics (contact rail, outcome tracking, cold-start, demand-posting), the child-safety/legal stack (lawful basis, COPPA, AB 488, CSAM reporting, scout vetting), monetization (wrong-side pricing, donation-fee optics, club SaaS bundle, agent line), the competitive incumbents (Wyscout/Hudl, Tonsser, Snap! Raise, TransferRoom, Veo), the repo gaps (DSR/deletion, shadow tracking, notification infra, single-admin moderation), and the growth loops (return hooks, scheduler, shareable card, SEO/SSR, success stories). That is genuinely broad coverage. My findings are the operational-reality and platform-dependency angles none of them touched: seasonality, internal data correctness (as distinct from data coverage, which competitive did cover), the video-rail dependency, solo-founder incident-response latency, and accessibility. One folded angle worth a line: internationalization asymmetry — 16 leagues across 4 regions are TRACKED but donations launch US-only and there is no currency/locale/tax layer, so the largest supply-side geographies (English/European academies) have no monetization path and non-English families cannot transact even where the players live.

missing.title: Football's off-season silences the entire engagement engine for 6-10 weeks a year — precisely now
missing.why: Every recurring touch the platform has is computed off fixtures: AI weekly newsletters, player_pulse milestone cards, scout digests, and the 'your player just scored' alert all need matches to exist. Across the June-August summer break (and winter breaks in some leagues) there are no fixtures, so the newsletter has nothing to say, digests go empty, and pulse detection fires nothing — the product goes dark during the exact window when a solo founder is trying to convert a beta cohort. A scouting/tracking product that only speaks when games are being played teaches users to stop opening it for two months, and re-acquiring attention every August is far harder than never losing it. Nobody designed the off-season content mode (transfer-window tracking, pre-season friendlies, historical-season retrospectives, 'players to watch next season', academy intake news) that keeps the loop alive when the delta engine has no deltas.
missing.evidence: Newsletter + pulse + scout-digest all key off API-Football fixture deltas (pulse.py, weekly.py, scout digest 'delta engine'); today is 2026-07-16, mid-summer-break, so this is live right now. No off-season content mode exists in the roadmap ledgers.

missing.title: The verification moat rests on journey-sync classifications that are documented to be frequently WRONG — internal data correctness, not just coverage, is the trust risk
missing.why: The competitive analysts flagged that API-Football doesn't COVER youth football; the deeper, self-inflicted risk is that the data it DOES surface is repeatedly MISCLASSIFIED. The repo's own recent history is a run of correctness fires: loan-vs-sold mislabeling (#642, #643), a systemic 'released' mislabel affecting ~1375/1480 rows, and zeroed/hidden stats from current_club keying (scout-data-attribution ledger). The whole pitch is 'verified fixture-derived truth beats self-reported Instagram reels' — but if a player's page says 'released' when he was loaned, or 'sold' when he's on loan, or shows zeroed stats, the platform is publishing confidently-wrong data ABOUT A NAMED MINOR under a 'verified' banner. That is worse than an Instagram reel, because the reel never claimed to be authoritative. There is no visible data-quality SLA, confidence labelling, staleness indicator, or correction/dispute path when the sync gets a player's pathway wrong.
missing.why_consequence: the 'verified' brand is undermined by its own errors
missing.evidence: Commits 31f7dce/#643, f043c27/#642 (transfer resolver mislabeling), memory project_released_status_systemic_mislabel (~1375/1480 wrong), project_scout_stat_attribution (zeroed stats), ledgers CONTINUITY_transfer-resolver.md + CONTINUITY_scout-data-attribution.md.

missing.title: The showcase 'highlight reel' is a single third-party YouTube link — a revocable, rot-prone embed that quietly reintroduces the exact self-reported-reel weakness the moat claims to beat
missing.why: The curated reel is stored as a PlayerLink row holding a youtube_link string; the platform owns no copy of the footage and controls none of the hosting. Three concrete failure modes follow: (1) link rot — the uploader deletes or privates the video, or the channel is terminated, and the 'verified' profile silently renders a dead player; nothing re-checks embed liveness. (2) Bait-and-switch — YouTube lets the owner swap the video behind a stable URL after admin approval, so post-moderation content is mutable and un-reviewed. (3) It is the SAME primitive as an Instagram reel — an owner-chosen, owner-hosted clip — so on the showcase side the differentiator vs 'self-reported reels' is thin: only Film Room footage is genuinely club-vouched, and that rail is concierge-only and billing-unwired. Betting the single organic-video surface on one external platform's ToS, availability, and 'made-for-kids' embedding restrictions (YouTube disables key embed features on kids' content) is an un-hedged dependency.
missing.why_consequence: dead/mutable reels erode the verification story on the supply side
missing.evidence: academy-watch-backend/src/models/showcase.py (reel reuses PlayerLink link_type='highlight'), league.py:654 youtube_link String(500); no liveness re-check or copy-hosting in the model.

missing.title: Solo-founder incident response can't meet the hours-not-days SLA that money movement AND child-safety reports both demand
missing.why: Two of the highest-stakes interaction types on the roadmap require rapid HUMAN action, and a one-person operation structurally cannot guarantee it. (1) Safeguarding: once any contact/claim surface exists, a report that 'an adult is contacting my child' or 'a stranger claimed my kid's profile' must be actioned in hours — a queue that clears 'when the admin happens to log in' is the difference between a near-miss and a headline. (2) Money: Stripe Connect donations and pay-per-match introduce chargebacks, refund demands, disputed payouts, and failed-transfer support — all time-boxed by Stripe's evidence windows, and all landing on the same single admin who also approves claims, moderates content, and runs the football data pipeline. There is no support inbox/ticketing, no on-call/escalation path, no coverage plan for when the founder is asleep, travelling, or ill, and no documented incident-response runbook for a safeguarding or breach event. At the moment self-listing and donations actually get traction, the founder becomes a single point of failure for legally time-sensitive work.
missing.why_consequence: a time-critical safety or payment incident goes unhandled
missing.evidence: Repo-audit already noted single-admin, pre-publication-only moderation with no user report queue; no support/ticketing, escalation, or incident-runbook artifacts exist in docs/agents or ledgers; Stripe Connect + donations are on the roadmap.

missing.title: No accessibility posture — a consumer subscription/donation web product with a June-2025 EU obligation and a natural disability-discrimination surface
missing.why: The platform is a pure client-rendered SPA with no stated WCAG/accessibility work, yet it sells (or will sell) subscriptions and process donations to consumers, and ships a native iOS app. The European Accessibility Act's requirements became applicable on 28 June 2025 for consumer digital services (e-commerce, and services offered to EU consumers), and the Scout Pro subscription plus any EU-facing flow plausibly fall in scope; in the US, ADA Title III web-accessibility suits against consumer sites are a well-established litigation pattern, and public-facing youth/education-adjacent products draw scrutiny. Beyond compliance, the audience includes coaches, parents, and scouts who use screen readers or need keyboard navigation, and an inaccessible donate/checkout flow simply loses that revenue. Accessibility was not raised by any prior analyst and there is no audit, statement, or remediation plan.
missing.why_consequence: regulatory exposure plus lost/blocked users at checkout
missing.evidence: Frontend is React/Vite SPA (CLAUDE.md tech stack); no a11y/WCAG references in docs/agents/frontend.md scope or ledgers; European Accessibility Act applicable 2025-06-28.
